prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Booking Holdings Inc." (ticker BKNG), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BKNG", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Booking Holdings Inc.
result.industry: Online travel agencies and travel metasearch
markets: Online flight, car-rental and attraction booking

mission.statement: Our mission is to make it easier for everyone to experience the world.
mission.plain: Make travel simple so anyone can go and see the world.

about.plain: Booking Holdings runs websites and apps like Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda and KAYAK where people find and book places to stay, flights, rental cars and things to do. Hotels and home owners list their rooms there, and Booking takes a cut of each stay it sells. It also runs OpenTable, which lets you reserve a table at a restaurant. In 2025 people booked about 1.2 billion room-nights through it.
about.customers: Travellers all over the world book through it, and hotels, home owners, airlines and restaurants pay it to bring them customers.
about.everyday: If you have ever booked a hotel on Booking.com or compared flight prices on KAYAK, you have used Booking Holdings.

money.part: Bookings it handles the payment for (merchant)
money.plain: hotel stays, flights, cars and activities where Booking takes the traveller's payment
a fee hotels pay when a guest pays the hotel directly
ads on KAYAK and restaurant booking tools at OpenTable
plane tickets and tours sold alongside hotels; flight tickets grew 37% in 2025
AI trip planners and assistants that could plan and book a whole trip for you

result.summary: Booking has a wide moat built on a two-sided network: about 4.4 million properties (3.9 million alternative homes) attract the most travellers, and those travellers keep hotels listing, which funds the largest performance-marketing budget in travel ($8.2B in 2025). Its scale gives it 35%+ adjusted EBITDA margins that smaller rivals cannot match, though it depends on Google for traffic and faces regulators and AI assistants that could reroute demand.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue as a share of gross bookings edged up from about 14.3% in 2024 ($23.7B/$165.6B) to 14.5% in 2025 ($26.9B/$186.1B) while room nights still grew 8% to 1,235M, showing hotels accept its commissions; but European regulators (DMA gatekeeper designation, Spain's €413.2M CNMC fine, under appeal) have curbed parity clauses, limiting further fee increases.

moats.evidence: Booking.com is the world's leading online accommodation brand by room nights (per its 10-K), and its brand lets it win more direct and app traffic each year, reducing paid-search dependence.
Travellers can compare prices elsewhere in seconds; Genius loyalty and stored payments add only mild stickiness, while hotels list on many channels at once.
About 4.4 million listed properties (Dec 2025) draw the most travellers (1,235M room nights in 2025), and that demand makes it the channel hotels cannot skip, a classic two-sided marketplace.

With $186.1B of 2025 gross bookings versus Expedia's $119.6B, Booking spreads its $8.2B marketing budget and technology over more transactions, earning a 32.8% operating margin versus Expedia's 12.7%.
Global OTA hotel booking has consolidated into a few players (Booking, Expedia, Trip.com, Airbnb), leaving little room for new entrants at scale.
Its agency model with pay-at-hotel was once hard for merchant-model rivals to copy, but competitors have long since matched it.
Decades of test-and-learn culture and performance-marketing bidding skill give it superior return on ad spend, though this know-how is not unique in principle.
It has no exclusive supply; hotels and homes can list on any platform.

customers.evidence: Travellers keep returning (record 1,235M room nights in 2025, with a rising share of direct traffic and Genius loyalty members), but consumer-review sites show many complaints about customer service, and hotel partners often resent commission levels.

talent.evidence: About 24,300 employees (Dec 2025) in a tech hub in Amsterdam with good pay, but the company is not a fixture on major best-employer lists and its 2025-2027 transformation program cut costs and jobs.

product.evidence: Booking.com offers the broadest accommodation inventory (about 4.4M properties including 3.9M alternative homes) with free-cancellation and pay-later options, and has added AI trip planners and partner tools such as Smart Messenger.

competitors.name: Expedia Group
competitors.note: Global OTA (Expedia, Hotels.com, Vrbo) competing in hotels, homes, flights, cars and B2B travel.

competitors.name: Airbnb
competitors.note: Leader in alternative accommodations, where Booking.com is pushing hard; expanding into hotels and experiences.

competitors.name: Trip.com Group
competitors.note: Dominant in China and growing in Asia and Europe; rivals Agoda and Booking.com in Asia-Pacific.

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Travel, Gemini)
competitors.note: Google Hotels/Flights and Gemini AI capture travel searches and are Booking's main paid-traffic source; named as a competitor in the 10-K.

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: AI assistants (ChatGPT agents) could become the starting point for trip planning and booking.

competitors.name: Hopper
competitors.note: Private app for flights and hotels with price prediction, and B2B travel fintech.

competitors.name: MakeMyTrip
competitors.note: Leading OTA in India, a fast-growing travel market.

competitors.name: Meituan
competitors.note: Large hotel-booking business in China's lower-tier cities.

competitors.name: Tripadvisor
competitors.note: Travel reviews and metasearch, plus Viator for tours and experiences; competes with KAYAK and Booking attractions.

competitors.name: Marriott International
competitors.note: Hotel chains push direct booking through loyalty programs to cut OTA commissions.

competitors.name: Hilton Worldwide
competitors.note: Direct-booking push via Hilton Honors member rates.

competitors.name: Yanolja
competitors.note: Korean travel platform and hotel software provider expanding in Asia.

marketShare.market: Gross bookings of the three largest Western online travel platforms (share of their combined total)

threats: AI assistants (Google Gemini, ChatGPT agents) becoming the place where trips are planned and booked, cutting Booking out or forcing it to pay for traffic
Dependence on Google for paid traffic and Google's own hotel and flight products
EU Digital Markets Act gatekeeper rules and national antitrust cases (Spain's €413.2M CNMC fine under appeal, Dutch consumer claim over parity clauses) limiting pricing and ranking practices
Hotel chains steering guests to direct booking through loyalty pricing
Airbnb and Expedia's Vrbo competing for alternative accommodations, where Booking's room nights grew only 4% in Q2 2026
Travel-demand shocks such as the 2026 Middle East conflict, recessions or pandemics
Short-term-rental regulation in major cities reducing alternative-accommodation supply

ceo.name: Glenn D. Fogel
ceo.background: Wharton BS in economics, Harvard Law School JD; former investment banker and trader; joined the company in 2000 and led strategy and corporate development

c1.evidence: Booking is the leader of online travel booking ($186.1B gross bookings in 2025), but the industry is mature with growth slowing to high single digits in 2026 guidance, not an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Travellers choose it for the widest choice (about 4.4M properties), free cancellation and pay-later options, and that two-sided network scale is hard to copy and has lasted for two decades.

c3.evidence: Booking.com is a household name and the default hotel-booking site across Europe and much of the world, though reviews show customer-service complaints that temper recommendations.

c4.evidence: Its mission, 'to make it easier for everyone to experience the world,' is genuine but generic, and management communication focuses mostly on bookings growth, margins and buybacks.

c6.evidence: “convenient, huge choice, hotel deals, pushy” — the impression is mostly positive among travellers for convenience, but hotels complain about commissions and consumers about customer service.

c7.evidence: Global travel is a very large market still shifting online, with Booking's room nights up 8% in 2025, but growth is steady rather than a CRWD/NVDA-style secular surge.

c8.evidence: The Connected Trip adds flights (tickets up 37% in 2025), attractions (about 80% growth off a small base), payments and AI planning, but all remain inside travel.

m1.evidence: Fogel has articulated the Connected Trip and AI-agent travel vision for years, but it is an evolutionary vision for an existing business.

m2.evidence: Fogel is not a founder but has been with the company since 2000 and CEO since 2017, running it for the long term with steady reinvestment.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style beyond standard statements about partners and customers.

m5.evidence: Booking.com is known for a strong A/B-testing culture, but recent innovation (AI trip planner, Smart Messenger) is incremental rather than breakthrough.

m6.evidence: Fogel is a lawyer and former investment banker, not an engineer, and leads more on strategy and deals than on product.

m7.evidence: No scandals are tied to him personally, but there is no strong public record of a mission beyond running the business well.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Glenn Fogel at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Fogel keeps a low-key, conventional executive profile.

m9.evidence: Under Fogel revenue rose from $6.8B in 2020 to $26.9B in 2025 and operating margin reached 32.8%, while diluted shares fell about 21% (1,029M to 816M split-adjusted).

m10.evidence: A transformation program targeting about $650M of annual run-rate savings by end-2027 shows cost discipline, though the company is not famous for frugality.

c10.evidence: It helps hundreds of millions of travellers and small hotels worldwide (1,235M room nights in 2025), but improves convenience more than it transforms lives.

p2.evidence: Running a global two-sided marketplace at this scale is hard to replicate, but the product is a booking service rather than a deep technological feat.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025: $6,796M, $10,958M, $17,090M, $21,365M, $23,739M, $26,917M (2020 itself fell due to the pandemic).

f2.evidence: Booking reports no gross margin, but operating margin rose from -9.3% in 2020 to 22.8% (2021), 29.9% (2022), 27.3% (2023), 31.8% (2024) and 32.8% (2025), with one dip in 2023.

f3.evidence: Debt of $20.2B versus cash of $17.2B (June 2026) is easily covered by about $9.5B of yearly free cash flow, but shareholders' equity is negative (-$10.8B) because of heavy buybacks.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from -$631M (2020) to $8,825M (2025) and operating cash flow from $85M to $9,409M, increasing every year.

v1.evidence: Booking.com is the go-to choice for its huge selection and free cancellation, but Expedia, Airbnb and Google offer similar prices, so it is not clearly better on every count.

v2.evidence: No top-tier best-employer ranking for Booking Holdings or Booking.com in 2025-2026 was found.

c5.evidence: Millions of travellers and especially small independent hotels and home hosts that rely on it for global reach would miss it, though Expedia, Airbnb and Google would fill much of the gap.
